sentences.text: Unlike other tyrannosaurs, Dryptosaurus possessed relatively long arms compared to more derived tyrannosaurs like Tyrannosaurus, similar to its relative Eotyrannus. This dinosaur was believed to have had large hands with three fingers and claws nearly 20 centimeters long.
Dryptosaurus is estimated to have been 7.5 meters long and weighed between 756 and 1500 kilograms. These estimates are based on partial remains of a single individual.
The specific name D. aquilunguis means "having claws like an eagle," referring to the three-fingered hand.
A famous painting by Charles R. Knight made Dryptosaurus one of the most famous dinosaurs of its time despite its poor fossil record.
Current efforts led by Gary Vecchiarelli aim to mount the Dryptosaurus skeleton permanently at the New Jersey State Museum in Trenton.

Fossils of Dryptosaurus were discovered by fertilizer miners in New Jersey within the New Egypt Formation. In the summer of 1866, workers from the West Jersey Marl Company found a theropod skeleton near Barnsboro, New Jersey, in the New Egypt Formation. Fossils of Dryptosaurus were discovered while mining glauconitic marl for fertilizer at the West Jersey Marl Company Pit.
The type specimen of Dryptosaurus is a fragmentary skeleton of a single adult individual cataloged as ANSP 9995.

Researchers suggest that Dryptosaurus likely used both its arms and jaws as weapons for hunting, capturing, and processing prey. Dryptosaurus likely used both its arms and jaws as weapons to hunt, capture, and tear apart prey.
Dryptosaurus likely preyed on hadrosaurids, ornithomimosaurs, and ankylosaurs.
Nodosaurids were present in the environment but likely hunted less frequently by Dryptosaurus due to their heavy armor.
The only known species of Dryptosaurus is D. aquilunguis.
The genus Dryptosaurus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877.
Dryptosaurus belongs to the clade Eutyrannosauria, which includes Tyrannosauridae and genera like Nanotyrannus but excludes more basal tyrannosaurs like Dilong.
Othniel Charles Marsh established the family Dryptosauridae in 1890 to classify large theropod dinosaurs including Dryptosaurus.
While earlier beliefs suggested Dryptosaurus had three fingers, Brusatte et al. (2011) noted the phalange shape suggests it may have had only two functional digits.

Dryptosaurus lived during the late Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 67 to 66 million years ago. Dryptosaurus lived in eastern North America during the Late Cretaceous period. Dryptosaurus lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 67 million years ago in the Maastrichtian stage.
Dryptosaurus fossils come from the marine New Egypt Formation, where dinosaur carcasses floated out to sea and were fossilized.
The type specimen was found in sediments deposited during the Maastrichtian stage of the Cretaceous, approximately 67 million years ago.

Some studies classify Dryptosaurus in its own family, Dryptosauridae, or within Nanotyrannidae. It is debated whether Dryptosauridae is a valid clade, as many subsequent papers recover Dryptosaurus as a basal eutyrannosaur outside this family.

In 2001, Chure argued that the holotype specimen AMNH 5780 probably belongs to Allosaurus rather than Laelaps trihedrodon. Most putative Dryptosaurus specimens from the Tar Heel/Coachman Formation are now considered indeterminate Eutyrannosauria separate from Dryptosaurus, with some suggesting they belong to Appalachiosaurus.
